title: Listen to a conversation.

I’ve been thinking about getting into bird-watching. Any tips?
Sure. A good pair of binoculars is essential. Instead of a guidebook, I’d recommend a mobile app. It helps you identify species and log sightings.
I actually have an old field guide, but it’s missing pages and doesn’t cover local birds.
Then get an app. Some of them even alert you when there’s a rare sighting nearby. That’s my favorite feature.
Impressive. I’d like to join a group too.
We’d love to have you. I’ll send you a link to our calendar of events, including local walks.

title: Listen to a talk on a science podcast.
transcript:
Nanoparticles are particles whose size is less than one ten-thousandth of a millimeter—super tiny. Nanoparticles have numerous applications. My family had a picnic last Saturday. We used sunscreen to avoid sunburn. Our sunscreen contains titanium dioxide, which has been used in sunscreen for decades. You used to end up with this horrible-looking white coating all over your skin while wearing it. But in newer sunscreens, titanium dioxide comes in nanoparticles. They block ultraviolet sunlight but are transparent, so the sunblock is completely invisible on your skin rather than smeary white.

Another example is silver. The metal silver has antimicrobial properties. The problem is, you can’t put regular metal on a wound, but with an ointment containing silver nanoparticles, we can actually use those properties to stop bacterial growth. We did that when my son scraped his knee at the picnic.

Humans have actually used nanoparticles for millennia. Take ancient Rome’s tesserae. Tesserae are tiny bits of highly colorful glass that the Romans arranged to create various images. Many Roman tesserae, especially pink ones, contain gold nanoparticles. The particles affect how light interacts with the glass and create the color. Did the Romans know what they were doing? They probably didn’t understand the physics of it, but some glass workshops realized that gold foil beaten to an extremely thin layer produces bright colors when heated between glass layers, and the technique was perfected and spread. Pink tesserae contained gold nanoparticles at between 10 and 30 parts per million. That’s so consistent that it’s definitely not random.

title: Listen to a talk in a music appreciation class.
transcript:
Have you ever wondered why music has such a strong emotional impact on us? Sometimes it comes from the way our brains respond to what’s called dissonance. Dissonance occurs when two or more notes clash. They sound together in a way that creates tension or instability. Imagine hitting two piano keys that are right next to each other. It creates a sound that feels unresolved.

Why does this matter? Music thrives on the tension between opposites. Dissonance is what creates a sense of unease that begs for resolution—to move to harmony. And when that resolution comes, say those two notes resolve into a harmonious chord, it feels like a breath of fresh air. This combination of tension and release forms the emotional push and pull of music.

Here’s something you might not know, though: the use of dissonance hasn’t always been welcome. There were long periods in European history during which dissonance in music was considered sinful by the religious authorities at the time. But then, in the 1700s, the German composer Johann Sebastian Bach came along. Bach started using dissonance more dynamically, and it became central to compositions. Today, modern genres like jazz and experimental music rely heavily on the unique emotions dissonance creates. Let’s listen to some modern popular music with some great examples.
